ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Natsume Sōseki — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for three weeks of epigastric pain with black stools and iron-deficiency anemia, with urgent gastroenterology referral for endoscopy

text.paragraph: New patient visit for three weeks of epigastric pain with black stools and iron-deficiency anemia, with urgent gastroenterology referral for endoscopy [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He has had stomach pain for weeks and his stools turned black; he wants to know whether it is cancer. [S]
He needs to finish the serial he is writing and fears that illness will stop him. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Natsume Sōseki, whose name was Natsume Kinnosuke, was born on the 5th day of the 1st month of Keiō 3 in the Japanese calendar (9 February 1867) in Ushigome Babashita-Yokomachi in Edo, now Kikui-chō in Shinjuku, Tokyo, the son of a town headman. [D]
At the age of one he was adopted into the Shiobara family; his adoptive parents divorced when he was nine, and he was returned to his birth family. [D]

After graduating from the English department of the Imperial University in 1893 he taught at Matsuyama Middle School and at the Fifth Higher School in Kumamoto, and married Nakane Kyōko, eldest daughter of Nakane Shigeichi, chief secretary of the House of Peers, after taking up the Kumamoto post. [D]
In 1900, at 33, he was sent by the Ministry of Education to Britain to study English for two years, and he returned to Japan in 1903. [D]
During his stay in Britain he soon felt at odds with the study of English literature and fell into a state of severe nervous distress, which continued after his return. [D]

The city of Shinjuku calls the London illness shinkei suijaku (nervous breakdown, neurasthenia), and the Sōseki museum calls it nervous depression; both are labels of the period or translations of it, not modern diagnoses. [R]

In 1907, at 40, he gave up all his teaching posts and joined the Asahi Shimbun as a staff writer, and about then moved to Waseda-Minami-chō; Sanshirō, Sorekara and Mon were serialized in the newspaper. He had made his name with I Am a Cat (1905 to 1906) and later wrote Kokoro (1914). [D]
From about May 1910, while writing Mon, he suffered from stomach illness, a gastric ulcer. [D]

Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: About three weeks of gnawing epigastric pain, worse before meals and at night and eased by food, with two episodes of black, tarry stools ten days ago and iron-deficiency anemia; stable, Glasgow-Blatchford score 4; peptic ulcer suspected and urgent endoscopy booked
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the diagnosis at endoscopy; its timing echoes his documented stomach illness of May 1910 (D).
Iron-deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 8 ng/mL)

value.displayName: Iron deficiency anemia secondary to blood loss (chronic)

list.item: About three weeks of gnawing epigastric pain, worse before meals and at night and eased by food, with two episodes of black, tarry stools ten days ago and iron-deficiency anemia; stable, Glasgow-Blatchford score 4; peptic ulcer suspected and urgent endoscopy booked: active, confirmed [S]
Iron-deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 8 ng/mL): active, confirmed [S]

Initial evaluation and safety: blood count, iron studies and metabolic panel; Glasgow-Blatchford score; stop ibuprofen and all NSAIDs and use acetaminophen; urgent upper endoscopy within three days; no acid-suppressing medicine or antibiotic before the biopsies unless bleeding recurs; call 119 or go to the emergency department at once for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, fainting, or severe pain. Guideline: ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection (2024); Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for peptic ulcer disease 2026 (2026); ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding (2021) [S]

Urgent gastroenterology consultation for upper endoscopy with biopsy within three days, to find the cause of the bleeding, exclude gastric cancer, test for Helicobacter pylori, and advise on treatment. Guideline: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for peptic ulcer disease 2026 (2026); ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding (2021) [S]

Iron-deficiency anemia: oral iron once the source is found at endoscopy; blood count about four weeks after starting iron and then every three months for a year; continue iron about three months after the hemoglobin is normal and until ferritin is replete; colonoscopy if the anemia does not correct once the ulcer has healed. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia monograph (2026) [S]

Stress and sleep: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and at the end of the episode; regular meals, a fixed bedtime, and writing hours that leave the evening free; counselling if scores rise. Guideline: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
Referral to gastroenterology, Kenji Abrahamsen-Ito, MD, ordered 1910-05-18 [S]
